note: Written to be spoken: one sentence or phrase per line; {"beat": s} is a deliberate pause; numbers are phrased the way they are said. `answer` plays after the learner answers a predict step.

lines: Your orders table has a hundred million rows... spread across a million pages. And there's an index on status.
You want the two percent that were refunded.
Two percent? That sounds small. So most engineers reach straight for the index.
But count the page reads... and the answer flips.
Let's predict it first.
Say every page read costs the same, and each page holds a hundred rows.
Up to what share of matching rows does the index read fewer pages than scanning the whole table?
answer: About one percent. One over the number of rows per page.
The next few steps derive it... and then show why real storage pushes it even lower.

lines: Here's the model. Aggarwal and Vitter, nineteen eighty-eight.
There's a fast memory that holds M items, and a slow disk that moves data in blocks of B items.
Work inside memory is free.
The only thing that counts... is how many blocks you move.
Three numbers describe any job.
N items in the problem. M that fit in memory. B per block.
Our table: a hundred million rows, a hundred to a page.
So it spans N over B... one million pages.
A full scan touches every block exactly once.
That's N over B reads. Here, a million... all sequential.
It's the floor for any job that has to look at all the data.
The index finds the matches fast. Its upper levels are almost always cached.
But every matching row lives on its own page, somewhere in the table.
So unless the table is stored in index order... each match costs about one random page read.
Now put them side by side.
The scan is flat, at N over B. The index climbs one read for every matching row.
They cross at one over B. Here, one percent.
CPU big-O can't see this. There, the index wins whenever the matches are a small part of the table.
Count block transfers instead... and it only wins below N over B matches.
At our two percent, the index reads twice as many pages. Try the slider.
Smarter engines sort the matches by page first, and read each page at most once.
Postgres calls that a bitmap heap scan.
It beats going row by row. But at two percent of the rows... you still touch about eighty-seven percent of the pages.
And real storage isn't fair.
A random read waits for a seek, or a fresh request. And a plain index scan waits for them one at a time.
Sequential reads just stream ahead.
If a random read costs r sequential ones, the crossover drops to one over r times B.
Postgres assumes r is four... so, a quarter of a percent.
And four is low on purpose. It assumes most random reads are already in cache.
On a cold hard disk, r is nearer two hundred... and the crossover falls to five thousandths of a percent.
Unless... the table is stored in index order.
Then the matches sit side by side, and k matches cost about k over B reads.
The index wins at almost any share.
Planners estimate this from a correlation statistic, from minus one to plus one.
Sorting on disk works the same way. Count passes, not comparisons.
External merge sort fills memory, sorts it, and writes a sorted run.
Then it merges many runs at once.
And that's optimal in this model.
Here's a terabyte, sorted with sixteen gigabytes of memory.
The first pass writes sixty-four runs.
The merge can take over sixteen thousand at once... so one more pass finishes it.
Two passes in total. Merging two at a time would take seven.
The same model works at every level of the hierarchy. Only the block size and the price of a move change.
CPUs move sixty-four byte lines. Databases move eight kilobyte pages.
Object stores want multi-megabyte ranges, because every request waits before its first byte.
So count the transfers at whichever tier dominates.
And the network is just another tier.
On a cluster, the slowest move is often between machines... and the same counting works.
Join a one terabyte table with a hundred megabyte one, on a hundred machines.
Shuffle both by key, and about nine hundred and ninety gigabytes cross the network.
Broadcast the small table instead... just under ten gigabytes.
The same join. The same work for the processor... and a hundred times less traffic.
Broadcast wins on bytes while the small table is smaller than the big one divided by the number of machines. Here, about ten gigabytes.
And only if it fits in every machine's memory.
So, back to the query.
Row by row through the index: two million random reads. At four times the cost... eight times the scan.
Sorted lookups: most of the pages, with gaps.
The scan: a million pages, in one sweep.
The real contest is between the last two... and that's exactly the call a planner's cost model makes.
At this scale, Postgres prices those two within about one percent of each other.
A close call... settled by details the deep dive works through.
Time to prove it.
Fifty million rows, fifty to a page, an unclustered index. Your query matches four hundred thousand rows.
Index, or full scan?
answer: It depends. The table is a million pages, and the index needs about four hundred thousand random reads.
If random and sequential reads cost the same, the index wins.
But at four times the cost, that's one point six million... and the scan wins.

lines: Next. Sort four terabytes, with eight gigabytes of memory, and eight megabyte blocks.
How many passes over the data?
answer: The first pass writes five hundred and twelve runs. The merge can take over a thousand at once... so one more pass does it.

lines: Last one. Our terabyte sort again... but memory is cut to a quarter.
What happens?
answer: Two hundred and fifty-six runs, and the merge can take over four thousand at once.
Memory only starts to matter once the runs outnumber what you can merge.
